title: THREE WOMEN CHRISTIANS OFTEN MERGE INTO ONE—AND SCRIPTURE DOESN’T
paragraphs:
THREE WOMEN CHRISTIANS OFTEN MERGE INTO ONE—AND SCRIPTURE DOESN’T
Mary Magdalene was not called a prostitute. The woman caught in adultery was never named Mary. And the woman who washed Jesus’ feet with her tears has a story powerful enough that we should stop rewriting it.
There is a woman in the Bible almost everyone thinks they know.
She is usually imagined with a scandalous past.
A prostitute.
A woman caught in adultery.
A woman weeping at Jesus’ feet.
An alabaster jar breaking open.
Long hair wiping away tears and perfume.
Seven demons.
Then resurrection morning.
And somewhere through centuries of sermons, paintings, films, traditions, and retellings, all those images began wearing one face.
Mary Magdalene.
There is only one problem.
Scripture never puts all of those stories on Mary Magdalene.
Read the Gospels slowly and something startling happens.
The woman begins to separate.
Then another woman appears.
Then another.
And suddenly we discover that some of the most familiar things Christians have repeated about Mary Magdalene were never actually said about her in the biblical text.
This matters for more than correcting a Bible trivia mistake.
Because whenever we add something to another person’s story that God did not put there, we risk remembering a label more clearly than we remember the grace of Christ.
And maybe that cuts closer to home than we expect.
Because some of us know what it feels like when people merge the worst thing they heard about us with who we actually are.
One failure becomes your identity.
One rumor becomes your biography.
One season becomes your name.
One sin follows you into rooms you entered years after repentance.
People remember what you were.
Jesus knows who you are.
So before we talk about these women, hear the question beneath the question:
What if you have been carrying a version of someone’s story that Scripture itself never tells?
Go first to Luke 7.
Jesus is eating in the house of a Pharisee named Simon when a woman enters.
Luke does not call her Mary.
Luke does not call her Magdalene.
Luke does not call her an adulteress.
Luke describes her with the Greek words:
γυνὴ … ἁμαρτωλός — gynē … hamartōlos
A woman who was known in the city as sinful.
That is what the text gives us.
Not “prostitute.”
Not “Mary Magdalene.”
Not “the adulterous woman from John 8.”
A sinful woman.
And there is something painfully human about the scene.
She walks into a house where she knows people know her reputation.
Imagine that walk.
Imagine crossing a doorway while knowing what the people around the table think about you.
Imagine feeling eyes follow you.
Imagine knowing that before you say one word, somebody in that room has already reduced your entire existence to the thing you did.
She carries an alabaster flask of perfume.
Then she stands behind Jesus.
And she breaks.
Not the jar yet.
Her.
She weeps.
Her tears fall onto His feet.
She wipes His feet with her hair.
She kisses them.
She pours perfume over them.
And Simon watches.
But Simon does not see what Jesus sees.
Simon sees a category.
Jesus sees a woman.
Simon sees contamination.
Jesus sees faith.
Simon sees her history.
Jesus sees what grace is doing in the present.
Luke records Simon thinking that if Jesus were truly a prophet, He would know what kind of woman was touching Him.
But Jesus does know.
That is precisely the point.
Christ's holiness is not preserved by ignorance of sinners.
He knows exactly who approaches Him.
He knows what she has done.
He knows what you have done.
There has never been a confession that surprised Him.
There has never been a hidden browser history that shocked Him.
There has never been an addiction He discovered too late.
There has never been a betrayal, affair, lie, secret, relapse, private compromise, or carefully protected darkness that made Jesus suddenly reconsider whether His blood was sufficient.
He already knows.
And still He receives repentant sinners.
Jesus tells Simon about two debtors whose debts are canceled. Then He turns toward the woman while speaking to the Pharisee.
That detail is devastating.
He looks at the person everyone is judging while confronting the person doing the judging.
Then comes the heart of the scene.
Jesus tells her that her sins are forgiven and concludes:
Ἡ πίστις σου σέσωκέν σε· πορεύου εἰς εἰρήνην.
Hē pistis sou sesōken se; poreuou eis eirēnēn.
“Your faith has saved you; go in peace.”
Notice where salvation rests.
Not in the perfume.
Not in the tears as though enough crying purchases forgiveness.
Not in public humiliation.
Not in her ability to punish herself for her past.
Jesus points to faith.
Her love is the overflowing evidence of forgiven debt, not a payment large enough to force God to forgive.
That distinction is the Gospel.
We do not purchase grace with remorse.
We do not make ourselves clean enough for Christ.
We come bankrupt.
Christ forgives.
Grace creates love.
Forgiveness produces worship.
The forgiven heart stops calculating how little it can give Jesus.
And perhaps somebody reading this has spent years trying to repay God for what Jesus already carried to the cross.
You keep punishing yourself because guilt feels more spiritual than grace.
You believe Jesus forgives sinners in general, but when your own memories wake up at two in the morning, you quietly add an exception.
Me.
Maybe others.
But not me.
Listen again.
“Your faith has saved you; go in peace.”
Jesus does not say, “Go pretend it never happened.”
Grace is not amnesia.
He does not say sin was harmless.
Grace never needs to lie about evil in order to defeat it.
He forgives.
That is infinitely better.
The Gospel does not say your sin was insignificant.
The Gospel says the Son of God considered your redemption worth His blood.
And then Luke does something extraordinarily important.
The chapter ends.
Luke 8 begins.
Jesus travels from town to town proclaiming the kingdom of God. The Twelve are with Him, along with women who had been healed.
And now Luke names one:
Μαρία ἡ καλουμένη Μαγδαληνή
Maria hē kaloumenē Magdalēnē.
“Mary, the one called Magdalene.”
Luke then says:
ἀφ’ ἧς δαιμόνια ἑπτὰ ἐξεληλύθει
“from whom seven demons had gone out.”
This is Mary Magdalene.
Notice what Luke does not say.
He does not say, “the sinful woman mentioned above.”
He does not say she was a prostitute.
He does not say she committed adultery.
He identifies her as Mary called Magdalene and tells us that seven demons had gone out from her.
Seven demons are not biblical shorthand for prostitution.
Demonic affliction and sexual immorality are not interchangeable categories.
We should not turn one into the other merely because later imagination found the combination dramatic.
Mary Magdalene’s actual biblical story is already astonishing.
She had known terrible bondage.
Jesus delivered her.
She followed Him.
She became part of the circle of women supporting Jesus and His ministry from their resources.
She remained near the crucifixion when so much seemed lost.
She witnessed where Jesus was laid.
And in John’s Gospel, she encounters the risen Christ.
Why would we need to manufacture another scandal for her?
Is deliverance from seven demons not enough?
Is standing near the cross not enough?
Is weeping outside an empty tomb not enough?
Is hearing the risen Jesus call her by name not enough?
Mary’s greatness is not improved by inventing a darker résumé.
Grace does not need exaggeration.
Jesus does not become more glorious when we make somebody else look worse.
Then there is another woman Christians sometimes pull into this composite portrait.
The woman caught in adultery in John 7:53–8:11.

Whatever discussion Christians have about the textual history of that passage—and responsible modern Bibles openly note that the earliest manuscripts do not contain it—one fact is straightforward within the story as transmitted:
the woman is not named Mary Magdalene.
She is not named Mary of Bethany.
She is simply the woman brought before Jesus.
Dragging her into Mary Magdalene’s biography requires information the text never supplies.
And even inside that famous scene, notice what Christ refuses to do.
He does not join the mob.
But neither does He baptize sin as righteousness.
Mercy and holiness meet.
“Neither do I condemn you” is followed by the command to leave the life of sin.
That is the Jesus our generation desperately needs to encounter.
Not a Christ redesigned into mere affirmation.
Not a Christ reduced to condemnation.
The real Christ.
Full of grace and truth.
The Christ who receives sinners and calls sinners out of sin.
The Christ who does not throw repentant people away and does not tell them their chains are freedom.
Grace does not mean Jesus leaves you exactly where He found you.
Grace means He loves you too deeply to do that.
Then another familiar scene appears near the end of Jesus’ earthly ministry.
Bethany.
Perfume.
Jesus.
A woman.
Hair.
Feet.
And this is where careful reading matters enormously.
John names this woman.
She is Mary of Bethany, sister of Martha and Lazarus.
John 12:3 begins:
ἡ οὖν Μαριὰμ λαβοῦσα λίτραν μύρου νάρδου πιστικῆς πολυτίμου…
Mary takes an extraordinarily costly quantity of nard, anoints Jesus’ feet, and wipes them with her hair.
The house fills with the fragrance.
John had already identified her in connection with this act when introducing Lazarus in John 11.

Matthew and Mark also recount an anointing at Bethany shortly before the Passion. They do not name the woman; they describe expensive perfume being poured on Jesus’ head, and Jesus interprets the act in relation to His burial. John explicitly names Mary of Bethany in his Bethany account. Christians have long discussed how the Gospel accounts relate in their details, but Scripture gives us no warrant to turn Mary of Bethany automatically into Mary Magdalene or Luke 7’s unnamed sinful woman.
Three portraits have been collapsed again and again:
Luke’s unnamed sinful woman.
Mary Magdalene.
Mary of Bethany.
And sometimes a fourth story—the unnamed woman caught in adultery—is folded into the same imagined biography.
But Scripture does not tell us to do that.
And something beautiful happens when we stop forcing them together.
Each woman gets her testimony back.
The unnamed woman of Luke 7 gets to remain what the Gospel makes her: a forgiven sinner whose faith erupts into extravagant love.
Mary Magdalene gets her testimony back: a woman dramatically delivered by Christ who faithfully follows Him and becomes a witness to the risen Lord.
Mary of Bethany gets her testimony back: a devoted disciple whose costly act of love points toward Jesus’ approaching burial.
The woman accused of adultery gets to remain unnamed rather than having someone else’s identity attached to her.
And Jesus stands at the center of every story.
That may be the deepest correction of all.
Because Christianity was never supposed to be obsessed with constructing scandalous biographies about broken people.
Christianity is about Jesus Christ.
We keep staring at the women.
The Gospel keeps directing us toward the Savior.
Who forgives sins?
Jesus.
Who casts out demons?
Jesus.
Who receives costly worship?
Jesus.
Who refuses self-righteous condemnation while calling sinners away from sin?
Jesus.
Who goes willingly toward burial?
Jesus.
Who dies beneath the judgment sinners deserve?
Jesus.
Who rises?
Jesus.
Who turns frightened, grieving, ashamed, wounded human beings into witnesses of grace?
Jesus.
This is why getting the story right matters.
Biblical accuracy is not cold scholarship fighting against heartfelt faith.
Truth protects people.
Truth protects testimony.
Truth protects us from turning tradition into Scripture.
And truth keeps Jesus at the center.
Maybe you have experienced the opposite.
Maybe somebody has merged several versions of you into one.
The addict you once were.
The marriage that collapsed.
The child you disappointed.
The pregnancy nobody knows about.
The years you wasted.
The church you walked away from.
The night you wish you could erase.
The secret that still makes your stomach tighten whenever somebody preaches about it.
And even after Christ began changing you, some people kept introducing you to themselves through your oldest chapter.
They remember the jar.
Jesus remembers the surrender.
They remember the demons.
Jesus sees the disciple.
They remember the accusation.
Jesus sees the person standing in need of mercy and transformation.
They remember your scandal.
Jesus knows what grace can write next.
But do not misunderstand this.
The Gospel is not, “You were secretly a good person all along.”
The Gospel is far more powerful.
We really are sinners, and Jesus really saves sinners.
Romans does not flatter humanity.
“All have sinned.”
The cross does not exist because human beings were misunderstood.
The cross exists because we were guilty.
Christ died for sinners.
He bore sin.
He rose victorious.
And everyone who turns to Him in repentance and faith is not merely given better public relations.
They are reconciled to God.
Forgiven.
Made new.
Brought from death to life.
That is why “From Scandal to Grace” is not a slogan about improving your reputation.
It is a declaration about redemption.
Jesus does not simply edit your image.
He transforms lives.
He does not merely help you hide the old chapter.
He gives you a new identity in Him.
He does not say darkness was light.
He brings you out of darkness.
He does not rewrite history by pretending sin never existed.
He rewrites what sin thought the ending would be.
The cross looked like scandal.
Then Sunday came.
A sealed tomb looked final.
Then the stone moved.
Mary Magdalene stood weeping because she thought the body of Jesus was gone.
Then a voice said her name.
“Mary.”
Imagine that moment.
The woman once tormented by seven demons hears the risen Lord speak her name.
Not her affliction.
Her name.
And perhaps that is where this entire article has been trying to take you.
Beyond correcting a misconception.
Beyond Greek vocabulary.
Beyond identifying which Mary did what.
To this:
Jesus knows your name more deeply than your scandal does.
Your sin must be confessed, not romanticized.
Your chains must be broken, not renamed.
Your past must be surrendered, not worshiped.
But none of those things possesses greater authority than the crucified and risen Son of God.
If you are hiding, come into the light.
If you have sinned, repent.
If you have wandered, return.
If shame keeps whispering that Jesus will receive everybody except you, stop trusting shame as though shame were a theologian.
Look at Christ.
The woman in Luke 7 came carrying a reputation and left hearing about peace.
Mary Magdalene knew oppression and became a follower and resurrection witness.
Mary of Bethany poured out something precious before the One who was about to pour out His life.
Different women.
Different stories.
The same Savior.
And that Savior is still saving.

If this exposed something you have believed for years, don't be embarrassed that you learned something. Open the Bible again. Test everything against Scripture. Let the Word correct what tradition, movies, sermons, memes, and even sincere teachers may have blurred.
And if this reached deeper than biblical history—if it touched the part of you that is exhausted from being remembered only by your worst chapter—be honest.
You do not have to explain everything publicly.
Sometimes three words are enough to tell another believer, “Please stand with me.”
Then send this to somebody who has been crushed by a label.
It doesn't.
Christ does.
Luke 8:1–3. John 11–12. Matthew 26:6–13. Mark 14:3–9. Read them slowly. Compare them. Let Scripture speak with its own voice.
Grace cannot be bought. Give freely, prayerfully, and willingly.
Open the Scriptures.
Know the real Jesus.
Repent when His Word exposes you.
Receive the grace He purchased at the cross.
Tell somebody what He has done.
Because the world does not need a more sensational Mary Magdalene.
It needs the Christ Mary Magdalene actually followed.
It needs the Jesus who forgives sinners without pretending sin is harmless.
The Jesus who breaks chains.
The Jesus who receives worship.
The Jesus who went willingly to His burial.
The Jesus whose tomb could not keep Him.
The Jesus who still calls broken people by name.
Share Him.
Follow Him.
And when somebody tries to reduce you forever to the chapter Christ has redeemed, remember this:
People may keep calling you by your scandal long after Jesus has called you by your name.
